studies.title: Are Those Who Know Equal
studies.meaning: The comparison is deliberately left unfinished. One side is described closely, a person devout through the watches of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of what is coming and hoping for mercy, and the other side is never described at all. Then the question changes shape. Instead of asking whether the devout and the heedless are equal, it asks whether those who know and those who do not are equal, so the two pairs are quietly identified with each other and the reader is left to complete it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat immediately before this describe someone who calls on God in trouble and forgets the whole episode once relief arrives. This ayah sets the opposite case beside that one without naming the first party again, which is why the comparison reads as though half of it has been removed. The surah addresses people who conceded God's existence and let the concession change nothing.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning sustained obedience, and used specifically of long standing in prayer. It describes duration rather than intensity, which fits an ayah measuring a person by hours rather than moments.
The divisions of the night as that society counted them. Using the plural places the devotion across the night rather than at one point in it, without naming any particular watch.
Caution taken by someone who has understood a danger, not fright. It is the alertness of a traveller in bad country, and it sits here in the same clause as hope without either cancelling the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night was long, unlit, and divided into named watches that people used to organise sleep and guard duty. Standing through them cost sleep in a society where hard physical work began at first light. Knowledge in that world lived in memory rather than on shelves, and a person was reckoned learned by what they could produce and apply, not by what they had read or owned.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about those who know and those who do not is among the most frequently quoted lines in the whole Islamic scholarly tradition, cited in the openings of countless books. It does not occur in a passage about study. It arrives in the middle of a description of somebody praying through the night, and the link between the two is made by placement rather than by explanation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge is defined by what it produces rather than by what is held. The person described knows something in the sense that they act on it at an hour when there is no audience, so knowing here means an understanding that has reached the body. Wariness and hope appear in the same clause, and neither is presented as the mature form that eventually replaces the other.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same connection from the other end, awe of God arising among those who have learned.
Describes the same night hours and the same two motives, and then adds what such people give away.
Shows the pattern in full, reflection at night on the heavens and the earth reaching a conclusion.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are sure is true and have not acted on. Not a large thing. Do the smallest act it implies before you go to sleep tonight: send the message, make the payment, throw the item away. This ayah treats knowing and doing as the same measurement, and one small action is enough to take the reading.

studies.title: God's Earth Is Wide
studies.meaning: Three statements, and the middle one is the one that surprises. Those who do good in this world have good; God's earth is wide; the steadfast are paid in full without any reckoning. Commentators have long read the middle clause as pointing toward leaving: if a place makes it impossible to live as you should, the world is not small. The last clause then changes the arithmetic. Almost everything else in this surah is counted precisely, and this alone is described as paid without a count being made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this point some of the community had already crossed the sea to Abyssinia and others were weighing it. The classical sources connect the clause about the wide earth with emigration in general rather than with any single decision, and the surah's setting supports that reading: it addresses believers under pressure in a city where they could not live openly as they wished to.

keyTerms.note: From a root joining beauty to benefit, so the verb covers doing right and doing it finely. What is promised in return uses the same root, which makes the sentence an echo rather than an exchange.
Room enough, from a root about capacity and ease. The same root gives the word for what a person can bear, so the width described is measured against what someone is able to do.

The word for arithmetic and for accounting, and also the word used of the final reckoning. Removing it here means the wage is not arrived at by a sum, which is unusual in a text that counts carefully.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your town in that world meant leaving your protection behind with it. A man away from his clan had nobody to answer for him, nobody to avenge him and no standing anywhere he arrived, so distance was exposure rather than freedom. Telling people in that position that the earth was wide was not travel advice. It offered a different protection in place of the one they would be giving up.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase about provision given without reckoning in several places and of several groups. What the commentators single out here is that it is attached to patience specifically, since patience is the one quality with no visible product for an observer to count. The reward without a sum is matched to a virtue that leaves nothing behind to add up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described as escaping measurement, which is striking in a text that elsewhere counts with care: a grain yielding seven hundred, an atom's weight brought into view. Removing the count for steadfastness says something about the quality itself, since it consists largely in what is not done. The middle clause then keeps the whole passage from collapsing into resignation, by naming an exit.

crossReferences.why: Poses the width of the earth as a question to people who stayed where they could not practise.
States the same thing in the first person and draws the same conclusion: My earth is wide, so serve Me.
Describes what the steadfast receive and the sentence they are said to say when trouble lands.

studies.applyIt: Find one situation you have been enduring mainly because you assumed there was no alternative. Spend twenty minutes actually checking: the cost of moving, the other job, what the conversation would involve. You may end up staying. The ayah places a statement about width between two statements about reward, and the width is the part most people never test.

studies.title: Do Not Despair Of Mercy
studies.meaning: The address does its work before any argument starts. People who have squandered themselves are still called God's servants, so the relationship is asserted before the problem is named. Then despair is ruled out, and the reason given carries no qualification at all: God forgives wrongs, all of them. The commentators read the ayah together with the two that follow, which call for turning back, so the openness described is the ground for attempting a return rather than a substitute for making one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report that this answered the fear of people who had committed grave wrongs before Islam and believed no turning back would be accepted from them. Several accounts are preserved and they differ over which individuals are meant. In the surah it arrives inside a warning about consequences catching up with people, so the opening is placed in the middle of the thing being warned about.

keyTerms.note: The word for running through property wastefully. Applying it to what someone does to their own soul borrows a picture from inheritance law: capital spent, with nothing to show for it.
A severe word for hope abandoned rather than merely low, used of someone who has stopped expecting anything at all. It is the state being forbidden here, not the wrongdoing that produced it.

A single word making the preceding noun completely general. It is what removes the category of exception a reader would otherwise supply, and it is placed after the word for wrongs rather than before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The word for excess belonged to the vocabulary of property. A man who ran through an inheritance was described with it, and he could lose his standing and the management of his own affairs to relatives who stepped in. Families knew such a man and spoke about him. Using that word for what a person does to their own soul put a familiar domestic figure into the sentence.
studies.didYouKnow: A number of classical commentators record this as the most hopeful ayah in the Quran, reporting the description as a judgement already in circulation rather than proposing it themselves. Its distinguishing feature is grammatical rather than rhetorical: one short word makes the term for wrongs entirely general, and no category of exception is named anywhere in the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims are made together. Forgiveness is stated without limit of scope, and despair is identified as the thing to guard against rather than as an appropriate response to serious wrongdoing. That reverses an instinct, since the person who feels their own case is exceptional is being told the sense of exception is itself the danger. The word used to address them settles the point before the argument reaches it.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same prohibition in a father's mouth after years of loss, and names who does despair.
Has Abraham ask the question directly, who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray.
Supplies what the commentators read alongside this, the instruction to turn back before the time runs out.

studies.applyIt: Write down, privately, the one thing you assume is past forgiving. Then read this ayah once, slowly, with that written in front of you. Notice which of the two you find easier to believe. You do not have to resolve anything today. The ayah's argument works on despair rather than on the wrong, and despair is the part still in your hands.

studies.title: Its Gates Are Opened
studies.meaning: The scene is built as a mirror of the one two ayat earlier, and the small differences carry the sense. Both groups are led in throngs, both reach gates, both are met by keepers. But there the keepers ask a question, and here they give a greeting, and the middle of that greeting is a single word meaning you have come out good. The commentators read it as a statement about a process ending rather than as a compliment: what needed removing has been removed, and the door is what follows.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing section of the surah, which takes its name from the throngs described in these two parallel scenes. The surah has argued throughout that people who agree about God's existence still divide over what follows from it. The ending stages that division physically, as two processions moving in opposite directions, and it is among the most sustained pieces of parallel construction in the Quran.

keyTerms.note: Successive crowds rather than one mass, from a root suggesting a small sound gathering into more. The surah takes its name from this word, which is used of both processions equally.
From the word for a storehouse and what is kept in it. The same term is used of the keepers at the other gate, so the office is identical and only the words spoken differ.
From a root covering what is wholesome, clean and pleasant, used of good soil and of a sweet smell. It states a condition arrived at rather than praising a performance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A walled town had gates and gatekeepers who decided who came in. Arriving late meant waiting outside until morning, and a stranger was questioned about his business and his people before the gate moved. Everyone travelling knew that pause at a wall. The greeting spoken here by the men at the gate is the ordinary greeting of peace, which is precisely what a traveller in that world most wanted to hear.
studies.didYouKnow: The two descriptions differ by one small connective in the Arabic, present in this ayah and absent in its parallel. Commentators have discussed it at length and read it in more than one way; some take it to mean these gates stood open before the arrival rather than being opened at it. Others treat it as ordinary style and draw nothing from it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Entry is described as arrival at a door rather than as a payment collected, and the last words spoken before it are a greeting. That the keepers pronounce them good on arrival, rather than at the start, presents the journey itself as what produced the condition for entry. The two scenes are given deliberately identical shapes, so an enormous difference in outcome is carried by very small differences in wording.

crossReferences.why: Gives the mirror scene, with the same procession, the same gates and a question instead of a greeting.
Shows the angels entering with the same greeting, naming what it is given for: peace, for your patience.
Sets both groups within sight of each other and lets them speak, which this pair of scenes does not.

studies.applyIt: The greeting at the gate in this ayah is the ordinary one, the same words you would use at a door. Say it properly to the next three people you meet: not muttered, not shortened, with your attention on them for the second it takes. It is the sentence this passage puts at the threshold of everything.
